newsitem.title: USA: Oil, wheat, lumber lead commodities lower.
newsitem.headline: Oil, wheat, lumber lead commodities lower.

text.p: Oil prices fell on Thursday as traders focused on growing fuel supplies rather than a fresh bout of winter weather in the U.S. Midwest and Northeast.

In other markets, wheat and corn prices fell on poor export business and lumber also fell. Overall, the Knight Ridder Commodity Research Bureau index of 17 futures contracts fell 0.44 point to close at 241.73.
Oil prices fell amid rampant rumours that gasoline cargoes from Europe were due to arrive this month in New York Harbour, a key hub.
"There are a lot of cargoes coming over carrying gasoline, so gasoline is taking a backseat," said Warren Tashnek, vice president of Fimat USA Futures in Houston.

Unleaded gasoline for February delivery fell 1.71 cents to 70.48 cents a gallon at the New York Mecantile Exchange. The steep decline sent February heating oil down 0.38 cent a gallon to end at 73.05 cents and February crude oil down 25 cents to $26.37 a barrel.

"Gasoline supply is very high in the midcontinent and supplies in the Gulf (of Mexico) have no where to go because the Harbour doesn't need them," said John Bradberry, vice president at Transmontaigne Products Services in Fayettville, Ark.
Talk of imports follows oil inventory data from the American Petroleum Institute on Tuesday showing gasoline stocks jumped 4.3 million barrels for the week ended Jan. 3.
Heating oil prices succumbed to gasoline's downdraft despite forecasts of cold weather in the Northeast, the world's largest heating oil market.
The National Weather Service's forecast for the six-to-10 day period from Jan. 14 to 18, issued on Wednesday, called for temperatures to be below normal in the Northeast.
But API data this week also indicated stocks of distillate, consisting of heating oil and diesel, grew nearly 3 million barrels.
"Part of the fall today has to be that we have had a pretty good move up recently, so it's natural to see some profit-taking," said Fimat's Tashnek.
March lumber futures fell the $10 daily limit to $412.80 at the Chicago Mercantile Exchange on continued weak demand at the start of the year.
"We came into the year with a lot of optimism and no business and the no business finally caught up with the optimism," said Curt Cunningham, president of Pacific Futures.
Traders said lumber mills have been hedging or selling futures contracts, an indicator that futures prices are attractive compared with the slow cash market.
Snows from the East into the Midwest overnight aided the protective cover on the soft red winter wheat crop, easing worries about possible damage from a freeze.
March wheat fell 5-3/4 cents a bushel to $3.89-1/4 at the Chicago Board of Trade.
"Exports were bearish and the concern over winterkill was overblown," said Steve Bruce of E.D. & F. Man International.
Net corn exports for the week ended Jan. 2 were also weak at 236,800 metric tons, below traders' expectations for 400,000 to 600,000 tons.
March corn fell 1 cent to $2.58-1/4 a bushel at the CBOT.
At the New York Coffee Sugar and Cocoa Exchange heavy speculator sales pummelled sugar prices for a fourth straight day, dragging the market to its lowest close in three weeks.
March world sugar ended down 0.15 cent at 10.72 cents a pound.
